short: A Mark V cut in half and lengthened to cross the Hindenburg Line's wider trenches.
full:
German trenches were being dug deliberately wide to stop tanks, and the Hindenburg Line's were wider still. The answer, worked out by the Tank Corps Central Workshops in France, was brutally simple: cut a Mark V behind the sponsons and weld in an extra six feet of hull. The stretched machine crossed a fourteen-foot gap and had room inside for a section of infantry or a pair of machine-gun teams. Metropolitan Carriage began building them new in May 1918, and 579 were finished by the armistice.

The Mark V* went into action at Amiens on 8 August 1918 carrying Lewis and Vickers gunners forward with the leading waves. The idea failed on its first outing: the men emerged after hours in the heat, engine fumes and pitching of an unsprung hull too sick to fight, and the practice was not repeated on that scale. As a fighting tank the type served through the Hundred Days, though the added length made it slower to turn and harder on its already overworked tracks.
